title: Matthew
subtitle: the Messiah, son of David, and his teaching for the church
lead: Matthew tells the story of Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel's story. It opens with a family history that runs from Abraham through David and the exile to "the Messiah," and it closes on a mountain in Galilee with the risen Jesus sending his followers to all the nations. Between those two scenes Matthew sets five long blocks of teaching, each ending with the words "When Jesus finished": the Sermon on the Mount, the sending of the Twelve, the parables of the kingdom, life together in the church, and the last things.

It is the most Jewish of the Gospels and also the Gospel the early church used most. Again and again Matthew says that something happened "so that what was spoken through the prophet would be fulfilled." Jesus is the son of David and the new Moses, the teacher who brings the law to its full meaning, and also "God is with us" (1:23), who promises at the end to be with his followers always. The book was written for believers in Jesus who were working out, in sharp debate with other Jews, what it meant to be faithful to Israel's God after the Temple fell in AD 70. Reading it with that setting in mind explains both its love for the law and its harsh words against the Pharisees.
facts: Anonymous. From the 100s the church named Matthew, the tax collector who became one of the Twelve (9:9; 10:3). Many critical scholars: an unknown Jewish-Christian teacher, perhaps one of the scribes Jesus describes in 13:52, "every scribe who has become a disciple for the kingdom of heaven".
Uncertain. Traditional view and some scholars: before AD 70. Most critical scholars: about AD 80–90, after the fall of Jerusalem.
Probably a city with many Jews and Gentiles, often thought to be Antioch in Syria; some suggest Galilee or elsewhere in Syria-Palestine.
A Gospel: an ancient life of Jesus (like a Greek or Roman biography), built around five great teaching discourses and full of Old Testament quotations.
Greek. Papias (about AD 120) said Matthew wrote in "the Hebrew dialect"; what he meant is debated.
authorship: Papias, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia Minor, wrote early in the 100s that "Matthew put the sayings in order in the Hebrew dialect, and each person translated them as he was able" (quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.39.16). Irenaeus (about 180) says Matthew wrote "among the Hebrews in their own language" while Peter and Paul preached in Rome (Against Heresies 3.1.1), and Origen and Eusebius agree. The ancient manuscripts carry the title "According to Matthew." Many Catholic, Orthodox and evangelical scholars still hold that the apostle Matthew wrote the Gospel, or that it rests on his witness. Only this Gospel calls the tax collector Matthew (9:9; Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 call him Levi) and adds "the tax collector" to his name in the list of the Twelve (10:3), which some read as the author's own signature.

Most critical scholars think the Gospel was written by an unknown Jewish-Christian teacher, not by an eyewitness. Three reasons are given. Our Matthew reads as Greek composed in Greek, not as a translation. It seems to use Mark, often word for word, which an apostle who had been there would hardly need. Traditional scholars reply that an apostle could well follow Peter's account as preserved in Mark, as Augustine already supposed. And its debates with the Pharisees and its picture of the church fit the years after AD 70. Papias may have meant a collection of Jesus' sayings, not this Gospel, or he may have meant "in a Hebrew style." The name Matthew may have become attached because the apostle was the community's founding figure or the source of some of its traditions.

Some scholars think an Aramaic or Hebrew collection by Matthew lies behind our Greek Gospel (a view argued in various forms by Catholic scholars and by others). A few defend the Griesbach view that Matthew was written first and used by Mark and Luke (William Farmer). Richard Bauckham argues that the Gospels rest closely on named eyewitnesses, which supports a link to Matthew without settling who held the pen.

audience.to: Communities of believers in Jesus, most of them Jews by birth, with a growing number of Gentiles, probably in a city of Syria such as Antioch, or somewhere in Galilee or Syria-Palestine, in the decades after Rome destroyed the Temple in AD 70. Many think they still kept the law; they knew the Scriptures well and counted on hearers who would catch an allusion to Moses, David or Isaiah. They met in their own gatherings, which Matthew calls the "church" (16:18; 18:17), and Matthew speaks of "their synagogues" (4:23; 10:17), as if the two groups had gone separate ways or were in the middle of doing so.
audience.why: After the Temple fell, Jews had to decide how to live faithfully without it. Teachers in the line of the Pharisees were building what became rabbinic Judaism around the study of the Torah. Matthew's community gave a different answer: Jesus, the Messiah, is the true interpreter of the Torah, and following him is the way to be faithful to Israel's God. So Matthew shows Jesus fulfilling Scripture step by step, teaching like a new Moses on a mountain, and keeping the law while explaining its deepest aim. He also prepares his readers to live as a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles, sent to make disciples of all nations. Knowing this audience explains why Matthew can be both the most Jewish Gospel and the one with the sharpest words against the scribes and Pharisees: it is a family argument among Jews over who rightly carries on Israel's heritage, not a Gentile attack on Jews. Later, when the church was mostly Gentile, some of those words were read as condemning the Jewish people as a whole, with terrible results (see 27:25).
views: Many scholars place the Gospel in Antioch, a large city with a big Jewish population where Jewish and Gentile believers first lived side by side (Acts 11:19–26; Galatians 2:11–14). Ignatius of Antioch, writing about AD 110, seems to know Matthew (he speaks of the star and of Jesus baptized "to fulfill all righteousness"), and the Didache, probably from Syria, uses a Matthew-like form of the Lord's Prayer.

Others (for example J. Andrew Overman and Anthony Saldarini) place the community in Galilee or nearby, in close contact with the early rabbis there after AD 70. They see Matthew's group as a Jewish sect, still inside Judaism, arguing with the leaders of what became rabbinic Judaism.

Scholars disagree on whether Matthew's community still saw itself as part of the Jewish people (Saldarini, Overman, Levine) or had already separated and saw itself as a new people (Graham Stanton, Douglas Hare). The answer changes how one hears sayings such as "the kingdom of God will be taken from you" (21:43).

A minority of critical scholars (Kenneth Clark in 1947, Georg Strecker and others) argue that the final writer and much of his church were Gentile Christians. They point to 21:43 and 28:19 and to 21:7, where Jesus seems to ride two animals, as if the writer misread the Hebrew parallelism of Zechariah 9:9. Most scholars answer that Matthew's command of Jewish law and Scripture points to a Jewish writer.

Scholars who date the Gospel before AD 70 (for example Robert Gundry, and many traditional readers) see the audience as Jewish Christians in Palestine or Syria still worshiping near the Temple, warned in advance of its fall.

outline: Who Jesus is: the family history, birth and infancy, John the Baptist, the testing in the wilderness, and the first disciples
First discourse: the Sermon on the Mount
Jesus' power: ten miracles, and the call of Matthew
Second discourse: the sending of the Twelve
Questions and opposition: John's question, the Sabbath, Beelzebul
Third discourse: the parables of the kingdom
Feedings, walking on water, Peter's confession and the transfiguration
Fourth discourse: life together in the church
To Jerusalem: divorce, the Temple, the debates, the woes on the scribes and Pharisees
Fifth discourse: on the Mount of Olives, the end of the age
The passion, the resurrection and the Great Commission

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Matthew against Second Temple Judaism, Roman Galilee and Judea and Herod's family, and asks what can be known of the historical Jesus. Used by historians of every background.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the Gospel was made: Matthew's use of Mark and of the sayings shared with Luke (often called Q), or the alternatives (Farrer, Griesbach, Matthew first), and its date and community.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads Matthew as a story: five discourses that end "When Jesus finished," fulfillment formulas, Jesus as a new Moses, and the frame of "God is with us" (1:23) and the promise of the last verse (28:20).

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Matthew as a Jewish book in a debate with other Jews after AD 70, with Jewish scholars on Jesus and on Matthew, rabbinic parallels, and an honest account of how passages were later used against Jews.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: How the church fathers, the creeds, the liturgy and the churches have read the passage. Matthew was the Gospel the early church used most.

sections.b:
Matthew is built for hearing and teaching. A prologue (1:1–4:25) tells who Jesus is: son of David and of Abraham, born of Mary by the Holy Spirit, God's Son named at the Jordan and proved in the wilderness. Then come five great blocks of teaching, each closed with "When Jesus finished" (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1), each following a stretch of story: the Sermon on the Mount (5–7), the sending of the Twelve (10), the parables (13), life in the church (18) and the end of the age (24–25). The passion and resurrection (26–28) crown the whole.

B. W. Bacon saw in the five discourses a "new Pentateuch," five books of Jesus to match the five books of Moses. Jack Dean Kingsbury pointed instead to the phrase "From then on Jesus began" (4:17; 16:21), which splits the book into three movements: who Jesus is, his preaching, his suffering and rising. Most readers use both. Listen also for the frame: the child called Immanuel, "God is with us" (1:23), and the risen Lord's last promise to be with his disciples to the end of the age (28:20).

Most of Mark is found in Matthew, often word for word, and Matthew and Luke share many sayings that Mark lacks. Most scholars explain this by the two-source theory: Matthew used Mark and a lost sayings collection called Q. Others think Luke used Matthew (the Farrer view, with no Q), or that Matthew came first and Mark used Matthew and Luke (the Griesbach view), or hold the church's old order, Matthew first (Augustine). The strongest point for the Farrer view is the "minor agreements": small places where Matthew and Luke agree in wording against Mark, as in Matthew 26:68 and Luke 22:64, which are hard to explain if each used Mark separately. Material found only in Matthew, such as the magi, is often labeled M. The notes point out where Matthew differs from Mark in a way that matters, such as John's protest at Jesus' baptism (3:14–15), without assuming one theory. See the topic page on the Synoptic problem.

Matthew quotes or alludes to the Old Testament more than any other Gospel. Ten times he pauses to say an event happened "so that what was spoken through the prophet would be fulfilled" (1:22–23; 2:15; 2:17–18; 2:23; 4:14–16; 8:17; 12:17–21; 13:35; 21:4–5; 27:9–10). Some of these were predictions in their first setting; many were not, but Matthew sees in them patterns from Israel's story that Jesus fills out. His quotations sometimes follow the Septuagint, sometimes the Hebrew, sometimes neither, which led Krister Stendahl to imagine a "school" of Christian scribes studying Scripture. The notes give the Old Testament wording, show where Matthew differs from it, and present Jewish and Christian readings of each text.

Matthew's Jesus says he came not to do away with the Law or the Prophets "but to fulfill them" (5:17), and that not one tiny letter will drop out of the Law (5:18). He tells the crowds to do what the scribes and Pharisees teach from "Moses' seat" but not to act as they act (23:2–3). At the same time he sets his own word beside the law ("You have heard ... But I myself tell you," 5:21–48) and makes mercy and love the key to it (9:13; 12:7; 22:37–40). Readers differ on what follows. Some think Matthew's Jewish-Christian community still kept the whole law, Sabbath and food laws included; others that Matthew sees the law as fulfilled and reinterpreted by Jesus for a church of Jews and Gentiles. The churches' own answers about the law and the Sabbath are shown on the pages of chapters 5 and 12.

Matthew is the most Jewish of the Gospels and also contains some of the harshest words against Jewish leaders: the woes on the scribes and Pharisees (chapter 23), the saying that "the kingdom of God will be taken from you" (21:43), and the cry of the crowd before Pilate, "His blood on us, and on our children!" (27:25). Read in their setting, these belong to a bitter argument among Jews after AD 70 over who rightly carries on Israel's heritage, much as Israel's prophets and the Dead Sea Scrolls denounce other Jews. Read later by a Gentile church, they were used for centuries to call the Jewish people as a whole "Christ-killers," and they fed contempt, expulsions and massacres.

Many churches have since rejected that reading. The Second Vatican Council declared that Christ's death "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today" (Nostra Aetate 4, 1965), and several Protestant churches have made similar statements, among them the World Council of Churches at its first assembly (Amsterdam, 1948), the Presbyterian Church (USA) (1987) and the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994). The notes on these passages give the Greek, the setting, Jewish scholars' readings and the history of their use, without softening what the text says.

Matthew stood first in nearly every ancient list of the Gospels and was the Gospel most quoted by the early church writers. Its forms of the Lord's Prayer (6:9–13), the Beatitudes (5:3–12), the words over the bread and cup (26:26–28) and the command to baptize "into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (28:19) shaped Christian worship. Its sayings about Peter (16:18–19), divorce (5:32; 19:9), church discipline (18:15–20) and the end (24–25) are still at the center of disagreements between churches; the "Where Christians differ" cards set the answers side by side.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Joseph as the first picture of the wise builder
spec.body: Matthew's Gospel ends with the call to make disciples by "teaching them to keep" all that Jesus commanded (28:20), and the Sermon on the Mount ends with the wise man who hears and does (7:24). I suggest Matthew already shows this ideal in Joseph, who never speaks a word in the Gospel but four times receives God's command in a dream and does exactly what he is told (1:24; 2:14; 2:21; 2:22). He is called "righteous" (1:19), the Gospel's key word for doing God's will, and his righteousness gives way to mercy toward Mary. If so, the prologue opens with a silent model of the obedient disciple, matching the eleven at the end who are sent to teach obedience. Commentators such as Davies and Allison and Raymond Brown note Joseph's prompt obedience; the link to 7:24 and 28:20 as a deliberate frame is my own suggestion and is speculative.

traditions.q: Does Matthew teach that the church has taken Israel's place (8:11–12; 21:43; 28:19)?
views: The church is the new People of God, but the Jews "remain most dear to God because of their fathers"; God does not take back his gifts and calling, and the Jewish people should not be presented as rejected or accursed (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 839–840). The Pontifical Biblical Commission (2001) reads Matthew's polemic as a dispute within Judaism in its own time.

The church is the true Israel, fulfilling the promises to Abraham, and the fathers read 21:43 of the kingdom given to the church of Jews and Gentiles. Orthodox teachers today generally reject blaming the Jewish people for Christ's death, while affirming that salvation is in Christ for all.

There is one people of God in all ages, the church, and Gentile believers are grafted into the one tree of Israel; 21:43 means the kingdom passes from unbelieving leaders to all who bear fruit. Many Reformed theologians, following Romans 11, also expect a future turning of many Jews to Christ.

No. God has two distinct programs: Israel, with national promises still to be fulfilled in a future kingdom, and the church. Sayings such as 21:43 concern the generation that rejected Jesus, and the kingdom offered to Israel was postponed, not cancelled. Progressive dispensationalists (Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock) see more continuity: one people of God in Christ, with Israel's national promises still to be fulfilled.

The church of Jews and Gentiles is the people of God through faith in Christ. Luther's late writings against the Jews (1543) are now repudiated by Lutheran churches, such as the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America's Declaration to the Jewish Community (1994), and Lutherans reject reading Matthew as a curse on the Jewish people.

reading: W. D. Davies and Dale C. Allison, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Gospel according to Saint Matthew (3 vols., 1988–97)
The fullest modern commentary, rich in Jewish background and history of interpretation.
A great commentary that traces how each passage was read through church history.
R. T. France, The Gospel of Matthew (NICNT, 2007)
Clear, careful and evangelical; strong on Matthew's use of the Old Testament.
Craig S. Keener, The Gospel of Matthew: A Socio-Rhetorical Commentary (2009)
Full of first-century Jewish and Greco-Roman background.
Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Zvi Brettler, eds., The Jewish Annotated New Testament (2nd ed., 2017)
Jewish scholars' notes on Matthew and essays on its Jewish setting.
Raymond E. Brown, The Birth of the Messiah (updated ed., 1993)
The classic study of Matthew 1–2 and Luke 1–2.
Dale C. Allison Jr., The New Moses: A Matthean Typology (1993)
How Matthew presents Jesus in the pattern of Moses.
Anthony J. Saldarini, Matthew's Christian-Jewish Community (1994)
Matthew's community as a group within first-century Judaism.
